questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a context diagram show?
options: One system as a single box surrounded by every other system it touches, with no internal detail, answering 'what does this system talk to at all'
Every object and field inside a single Salesforce org
The exact Apex code implementing an integration
A single piece of data traced through every system it touches in sequence
questions.explain: A context diagram zooms all the way out, showing one system as a single box connected to everything around it, answering the broad question of what it talks to without internal detail.

questions.q: Which diagram type does this lesson say answers the question 'what actually happens to this data' by following one specific record through every system it touches?
options: Context diagram
System landscape diagram
Data flow diagram
Org chart
questions.explain: A data flow diagram follows a specific piece of data (like a customer record or an order) through every system it touches, in sequence, which is exactly the view needed when diagnosing a data-quality or systems-of-record problem.

questions.q: What mistake does this lesson warn against when choosing which diagram type to show an audience?
options: Always using a context diagram regardless of audience
Showing an executive a detailed data flow diagram when they need a one-page context diagram, or vice versa for a fellow architect needing the full landscape view
Never using diagrams and relying entirely on written prose
Using color in diagrams, which the lesson says should always be avoided
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out mismatching diagram type to audience need -- an executive overwhelmed by a detailed data flow diagram, or an architect under-served by only a high-level context diagram -- as a common mistake.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is one disciplined habit that makes a landscape diagram actually useful?
options: Cramming every possible detail into a single diagram so nothing is ever left out
Labeling every connection with what's actually moving across it and indicating direction clearly
Avoiding any kind of legend or consistent shape convention so the diagram looks simpler
Drawing the diagram once at project kickoff and never updating it again
questions.explain: The lesson lists labeling connections with what's actually moving across them and indicating direction clearly as key conventions -- a diagram with unlabeled, undirected lines communicates far less than one that is explicit about both.

questions.q: What does this lesson describe as the predictable failure mode of a landscape diagram left unmaintained for years?
options: It becomes too simple to be useful
It accumulates boxes and arrows with no pruning, no legend, until no two readers would describe the same picture back to you
It automatically updates itself whenever a new integration is added
It becomes classified as Restricted under the organization's data classification scheme
questions.explain: The lesson describes the common failure mode as diagram sprawl -- years of added boxes and arrows with no legend or pruning -- and insists a System Architect must maintain these diagrams as living documents rather than one-time deliverables.
